newsitem.title: USA: U.S. blasts Serbia on election inaction.
newsitem.headline: U.S. blasts Serbia on election inaction.

text.p: The United States on Friday blasted what it called "hollow assurances" by Serbia of a commitment to democracy and issued a fresh warning that Belgrade's refusal to recognise opposition victories in recent elections would lead to Serbia's further isolation.

State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said these points were contained in a "very tough" message to Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic from Secretary of State Warren Christopher, who has concluded "events are moving in the wrong direction in Serbia."

Christopher, on vacation in California, sent the message after Yugoslav Foreign Minister Milan Milutinovic responded to a report by the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) on disputed November local polls in Serbia.
The OSCE report concluded that the opposition fairly won polls in 13 key provincial centres and in the capital Belgrade and called on Serbian authorities to accept the result.

Milutinovic acknowledged opposition parties had won a majority of votes in nine municipalities in Belgrade in the Nov. 17 local elections but said Serbian authorities needed more detail to clarify results in other towns.

Burns said Milutinovic's response "does not go nearly far enough," contained "hollow assurances ... of Serbia's commitment to democracy" and "fails to address seriously recommendations" in the OSCE report that could resolve Serbia's political crisis.

He reiterated that U.S. sanctions -- including a pledge to veto Serbia's access to international lending -- would remain in effect and said Milosevic should be concerned about "the consequences of increased isolation" from the world community.
U.S. officials apparently have not threatened any new punitive action against Serbia.

They said they believed a U.S. determination to maintain the existing so-called "outer wall of sanctions" on Serbia -- coupled with unprecedented continued opposition street protests in Serbia -- would eventually force Milosevic to act.
The outer wall of sanctions includes a U.S. pledge to vote against financing by the International Monetary Fund or any other international institution for Serbia.
"The consensus here is that the outer-wall of sanctions is working and we need to be patient and let internal (political) pressure on Milosevic grow," one official told Reuters.
Milosevic has been blamed for playing a major role in stoking the fires of Serbian nationalism and the Bosnia war.

But after he played a key role in achieving the 1995 Bosnia peace agreement, Milosevic, and Serbia, began to gain greater acceptance in the international community, including European moves to grant Belgrade trade preferences.

But U.S. officials say such welcoming moves -- which Milosevic desperately wants and needs to boost Serbia's ravaged economy and prestige -- have been withdrawn and there is now a united front with Europe against him.
Burns said Milutinovic's letter to the OSCE "contains defensive and legalistic justifications for the annulment of the November 17th election results."
Christopher's message urges Milosevic "to accept the election results, legitimise the election results in a fair way and legitimise the democratic will of the Serbian people."

It reiterates the U.S. call for a meaningful political dialogue between the Serbian government and the opposition and warns Milosevic "about the consequences of increased isolation should he fail to take sufficient action to correct the anti-democratic actions of his own government over the past month," Burns said.
Burns said Washington was not aware of any plans by Serbia to crack down on political opponents, who have staged six straight weeks of street protests over the elections.

But he warned "any resort to force by the Milosevic government would be a serious miscalculation and ... would find great opposition on the part of the United States and our allies." The administration believes Milosevic might have used force against the protesters if Washington and its allies had not spoken out firmly against such actions, he said.
